scLimbsCoveredByACT: NONE. The ACT corpus for SC 3.3.3 is empty: 3.3.3.json has actRules:[] (actRuleCount 0), testCases:[] (testCaseCount 0), testCaseCountsByExpected:{}, and there is no eval/act-augmented/3.3.3/ directory. So no limb of the SC is covered by any ACT rule or executable test case. Every coverage claim below is therefore about the 9 WCAG TECHNIQUES the inventory points to (not ACT rules/tests) plus 4 author seed patterns -- these are the only corpus-adjacent material.

(Techniques-only, NOT ACT) Core obligation 'the suggestions are provided to the user' is described by sufficient techniques G84 (text description listing allowed values / nearest allowed value), G85 (provide example, describe correct entry, or show similar valid values), G177 (suggested correction text / did-you-mean), and ARIA18 (alertdialog whose contents suggest how to fix), but only as authoring techniques with manual test procedures -- not machine-checkable ACT rules.

(Techniques-only, NOT ACT) Input-error type (b) 'input outside the required data format or allowed values' is well represented by G84 (limited set of allowed values), G85 (format/value/type restrictions), G177, PDF22 (PDF date/format fields), SCR18 and SCR32 (client-side format/type validation).

(Techniques-only, NOT ACT) Input-error type (a) 'information required but omitted' appears in G139 procedure (deliberately leaving a required field blank) and SCR32 ('All fields are required, except those marked optional').

(Techniques-only, NOT ACT) 'Provided in text' requirement -- G84 explicitly states an asterisk or red label is NOT sufficient and a text description is required; this is the one near-detectable limb (color/asterisk-only error) and matches the seed patterns' 1.4.1 cross-tagging.

(Techniques-only, NOT ACT) Proximity / locatability of the suggestion -- G177 (suggestion next to the field or a link near it) and G139 (mechanism to jump to errors) cover where the correction text must sit.

(Techniques-only, NOT ACT) Programmatic availability to AT -- ARIA18 (role=alertdialog, accessible name, focus management) is the only technique addressing whether the suggestion is announced/reachable by assistive tech.
scLimbsAbsentFromACT: The TRIGGER 'If an input error is automatically detected' has zero ACT rules and zero test cases. Nothing in the ACT corpus submits a form, triggers validation, and observes detection. Trusted Tester 5.G even gates 3.3.3 on 'Continue from Test 5.F' (an error must first be triggered) -- this dynamic submit-then-detect step is entirely unrepresented in any ACT artifact.

The PRECONDITION 'suggestions for correction are known' / TT DNA 'suggestions cannot be provided because they are not knowable' is absent. No ACT rule/test distinguishes a field whose correction is inferable from one where it is not, so the knowability gate is uncovered.

The CORE PASS/FAIL OBLIGATION 'the suggestions are provided to the user' -- the actual point of the SC (does the page tell you HOW TO FIX the error, the harder follow-up to 3.3.1's 'is the error identified') -- is met by NO ACT rule and NO test case. There is not a single passing or failing executable case for the obligation.

The SECURITY/PURPOSE EXCEPTION 'unless it would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content' (e.g. an incorrect password, per TT DNA and EN clause) is entirely unrepresented: no ACT case exercises a security-sensitive field where correctly WITHHOLDING a suggestion is the right outcome.

SUGGESTION CONTENT-QUALITY judgments from the Understanding are absent as ACT material: (1) listing the acceptable values ('Choose one of: January, February...'), (2) the did-you-mean conversion ('Do you mean December?'), (3) the nearest-similar valid value, and (4) an example/description of the correct format. Whether the provided text is an ADEQUATE / CORRECT suggestion (TT Evaluate-Results) is exactly the semantic judgment no ACT rule attempts.

The author-vs-user-agent SOURCE limb (Understanding: 'The content author may provide the description... or the user agent may provide the description based on technology-specific, programmatically determined information') is absent -- no ACT case covers the user-agent-supplied (e.g. native browser/PDF-viewer) suggestion path.

Programmatic ASSOCIATION of the suggestion to its field and live announcement on dynamic insertion (the 4.1.3-adjacent failure the seeds describe: error injected into a non-live, non-focused div) is absent from any ACT rule/test for 3.3.3.

ALL technologies beyond plain HTML form text: the PDF path (PDF22) and any non-web pattern are absent as executable ACT cases. The corpus has no ACT coverage in ANY technology because the rule/test set is empty.

Limited-allowed-value fields: month-name entry (Understanding '12' -> January..December), city-name lookup, bus-route trip planner with origin/destination autocomplete and select-box suggestions (G177).
Format-constrained fields: dates (SCR18 Date.parse, PDF22 MM/DD/YYYY, ARIA18 birth-date-after-hire-date), telephone, email, postal code.
Spell-check / did-you-mean search correction (G177 search resubmit on corrected spelling).
Client-side validation patterns: alert() dialog (SCR18), DOM-injected error list with in-page anchor links and focus management (SCR32), ARIA alertdialog modal (ARIA18).
Server-side validation patterns: re-display form with retained data plus a top-of-page text error summary and jump links (G84, G85, G139).

Real-world / framework domains from seeds (not ACT): WordPress builders (Elementor, Divi, WPForms, Gravity, WPForms), Wix/Shopify/HubSpot checkout, React conditionally-rendered error summaries, ARIA-antipattern forms with red-asterisk/red-border-only required+error state.
varietyGaps: BIGGEST GAP: there is no executable ACT material at all (0 rules, 0 cases). For a harness, 3.3.3 has nothing to run, score, or hand-label by outcome; it is a pure manual/LLM-judgment SC. Any variety must be synthesized -- the techniques are authoring guidance with prose test procedures, not pass/fail fixtures.

No FAILING cases exist anywhere. The whole SC is dynamic-failure territory (error message that identifies but does not suggest a fix; suggestion present visually but not in text; suggestion not announced). The techniques only model the POSITIVE/sufficient state, so there is no negative variety -- exactly where the SC's difficulty lies.

No success/failure SEMANTICS coverage: distinguishing a mere error identification (3.3.1) from an actual correction suggestion (3.3.3), and judging whether a suggestion is ADEQUATE/CORRECT, is the SC's core and is wholly unmodeled by any runnable artifact.

The security/purpose EXCEPTION has no representation -- no case where withholding a suggestion (incorrect password) is the correct PASS, so a checker/LLM has no exemplar of the legitimate no-suggestion outcome.
The required-but-OMITTED input-error flavor is under-represented vs the format/allowed-value flavor (only G139/SCR32 touch it), skewing variety toward format validation.

Trigger/interaction coverage gap: every limb requires submitting a form and observing post-submit DOM/AT behavior (live-region announcement, focus move, programmatic association). No ACT case performs this dynamic step; this is the seeds' central whyAutoToolsMiss point and the harness's 3.3.x/4.1.3 shadow-lane territory.

Technology variety gap: only plain HTML and one PDF technique; no native HTML5 constraint validation (required, pattern, type=email, setCustomValidity / :invalid), no aria-errormessage/aria-invalid/aria-describedby executable cases, no SPA/framework cases despite seeds calling them the dominant real-world failure surface.

Suggestion-SOURCE gap: no user-agent-provided suggestion cases (native browser bubble, PDF viewer alert) -- only author-provided text is modeled, despite the Understanding explicitly allowing the user-agent path.

aspects.title: Error identified in text but no correction suggestion given, though the fix is clearly knowable
aspects.description: This is the central, distinctive obligation of 3.3.3 versus 3.3.1: the page DOES identify the error in text (so 3.3.1 passes and any 'is there an error message' heuristic is satisfied), but the message stops at naming the problem and never tells the user HOW TO FIX it, even though the correction is plainly knowable from the field's constraints. Examples: 'Invalid date' with no format given, 'Password not strong enough' with no rules listed, 'Invalid entry' for a field that accepts exactly one of a small enumerated set. The required human judgment is twofold: (1) is a correction knowable here, and (2) does the present text actually convey it, or merely restate that something is wrong. A self-contained HTML page can be pre-rendered in its post-submit error state so no interaction is needed.
aspects.scLimb: Core PASS/FAIL obligation: 'the suggestions are provided to the user' (the harder follow-up to 3.3.1's 'is the error identified') when suggestions for correction are known.
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus for 3.3.3 is entirely empty (0 rules, 0 test cases), so there is no executable case for the pass/fail obligation at all. Automated tools at best detect that error TEXT exists (the 3.3.1 limb); they cannot judge whether that text contains an actionable suggestion versus a bare restatement, because both are valid non-empty strings. Distinguishing 'Invalid date' from 'Invalid date — use MM/DD/YYYY' requires semantic reading of whether a correction is present.

references.quote: 3.3.1 asks *"is the error identified & described?"*; 3.3.3 asks the harder follow-up *"does it tell you how to fix it?"*.
Suggestions for corrected input are provided, OR The description contains adequate information for the user to know what is required to fix the error.
persons with cognitive limitations may find it difficult to understand how to correct the errors. People with visual disabilities may not be able to figure out exactly how to correct the error.
Provide examples of the correct data entry for the field, Describe the correct data entry for the field, Show values of the correct data entry that are similar to the user's data entry

aspects.constructionStrategy: Pre-render each page in its post-submit error state (no JS interaction required to reach the failing view). Each FAIL page identifies the error in text (so 3.3.1 is satisfied) but the message is a bare restatement with no correction, while the field's true constraint makes the fix obviously knowable. Include at least one PASS twin per scenario family that adds the missing correction text (e.g. '...use MM/DD/YYYY') so the judge must distinguish presence-of-correction, not presence-of-error-text.
suggestedScenarios: Date field whose post-submit message reads only 'Invalid date.' with no format shown, even though the accepted format is a fixed MM/DD/YYYY (correction trivially knowable) — FAIL; PASS twin adds 'Use MM/DD/YYYY'.
Password field error 'Password does not meet requirements.' with the requirements existing in the validator but never surfaced in the message — FAIL.
A 'State' text field that accepts only the 50 two-letter US codes; on bad input the message says 'Please enter a valid state' without listing or hinting the allowed values — FAIL.
A quantity field constrained 1-10 whose error says 'Value not allowed' with no mention of the permitted range — FAIL.
A coupon-code field whose error 'Code invalid' could instead suggest the known format ('Codes are 8 letters, e.g. SAVE20FX') but does not — FAIL.
A username field error 'Username unavailable' where the system can compute alternatives (a sibling field already does) but here offers none — FAIL.

aspects.title: Suggestion text is present but wrong, misleading, or contradicts the actual validation rule
aspects.description: The page provides a confident, specific correction suggestion, so every 'a suggestion is present' check passes — but the suggestion is factually incorrect for this field: it names the wrong format, the wrong allowed range, a 'did-you-mean' value that is itself invalid, or a fix the validator will still reject. This is the direct analogue of 'alt exists but misrepresents the image.' Per Trusted Tester the obligation is that the guidance provides SUFFICIENT/ADEQUATE detail to fix the error; a misleading suggestion fails that even though text exists. Only a human who knows the field's true rule can detect the mismatch between the suggestion and reality.
aspects.scLimb: Quality/correctness of the provided suggestion: 'adequate information ... to know what is required to fix the error' / 'sufficient details for how to correct the error.'
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT case exists, and even a hypothetical one would assert on the presence of suggestion text, not its correctness against the field's true constraint. Automated tools have no model of what the field actually accepts, so they cannot tell that 'Use DD/MM/YYYY' is wrong when the parser only accepts MM/DD/YYYY, or that 'Did you mean January?' was offered for an input that was already valid. Correctness is a semantic, ground-truth judgment.

references.quote: Determine whether guidance provides **sufficient details** for how to correct the error and/or offers suggestions of corrected input.
The description contains adequate information for the user to know what is required to fix the error.
The conversion of the input data interpreted as a different month format, e.g., "Do you mean 'December'?"

aspects.constructionStrategy: Pages render an unmistakably specific, confident suggestion that is verifiably wrong relative to the field's own (visible-in-source) validation rule. The contradiction is internal to the page, so a judge with no external knowledge can confirm the mismatch by reading the stated rule and the suggestion. Provide a corrected PASS twin where the same suggestion is made accurate.
suggestedScenarios: Error 'Enter date as DD/MM/YYYY' shown next to a field whose validator (shown in source/help text) only accepts MM/DD/YYYY — following the suggestion guarantees re-failure.
Phone field error 'Use format 555-1234 (7 digits)' but the stated requirement is a 10-digit number including area code.
'Did you mean December?' suggestion fired when the user actually typed a perfectly valid '07' (July) — gratuitous and misleading suggestion.
Password error 'Must be at least 8 characters' while the visible real rule requires 12 — following the suggestion still fails.
Numeric range field error 'Enter a number between 1 and 100' but the field's documented rule rejects anything above 50.
Postal-code error suggesting 'Enter 5 digits' on a form whose stated locale (UK) requires alphanumeric postcodes.

aspects.title: Suggestion correctly WITHHELD for a security/purpose-sensitive field (exception that must read as PASS)
aspects.description: The SC explicitly carves out 'unless it would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.' A correct implementation of a security-sensitive field (login password, security-question answer, 2FA code, payment CVV) deliberately gives a generic, non-revealing error and offers no specific correction — and that is the right outcome, a PASS. The hard human judgment is recognizing when withholding a suggestion is correct (and must not be flagged) versus when the same generic message ('Invalid input') on a non-sensitive field is a real failure. This inverts the naive heuristic: here the absence of a suggestion is conformant.
aspects.scLimb: Exception clause: 'unless it would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content' (TT DNA: 'details about an incorrect password').
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus is empty and, per the survey, no case exercises a security-sensitive field where correctly withholding a suggestion is the right outcome. Automated tools cannot classify a field as security/purpose-sensitive, so they would either never flag missing suggestions at all, or wrongly flag the deliberately-generic login error as a failure. Deciding the field's sensitivity and whether the exception applies is purely contextual.

references.quote: Providing information about how to correct the error would **jeopardize the security or purpose** of the content (e.g., details about an incorrect password).
If an input error is automatically detected and suggestions for correction are known, then the suggestions are provided to the user, unless it would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.
unless the data is in a security related field where it would be inappropriate to retain the data for re-display (e.g. password)

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build PASS pages where a security/purpose-sensitive field deliberately shows only a generic non-revealing error. To force the discriminating judgment, pair the sensitive field with a non-sensitive field on the SAME page that also shows only a generic 'Invalid' (a genuine FAIL on that field), so the judge must apply the exception selectively. Include one over-disclosure FAIL where the author leaks security-sensitive guidance.
suggestedScenarios: Login form whose failed-login message is the correct generic 'Email or password is incorrect' (no hint which) — conformant PASS that a naive 'no suggestion = fail' rule would flag.
2FA code field error 'That code is not valid' with no detail about the expected code — correctly withheld, PASS.
CAPTCHA / security-question answer field giving only 'Incorrect answer' — correct withholding, PASS.
Contrast page: a sensitive password field with a generic message (PASS limb) alongside a non-sensitive 'ZIP code' field also saying only 'Invalid' (FAIL limb) — judge must separate the two.
Bank-transfer confirmation field whose error withholds the recipient's full account number for security — PASS.
Over-disclosure FAIL: a password field error that leaks 'Your password must contain the word from your security question' — the exception SHOULD apply but the author jeopardized security/purpose.

aspects.title: Correction not knowable: no suggestion required and absence must not be penalized (the DNA/precondition gate)
aspects.description: 3.3.3 only obliges a suggestion when 'suggestions for correction are known.' For free-form fields where the correct value is genuinely not inferable by the system (a free-text 'Tell us why', an open-ended display name, a one-time human-verified value), no specific suggestion is possible and the page conformantly provides only a generic 'This field is required' or 'We couldn't verify this.' The judge must decide whether the correction is knowable at all before deciding pass/fail — a precondition gate that distinguishes 'no suggestion because none is possible' (PASS/DNA) from 'no suggestion despite one being obvious' (the first aspect's FAIL). This is a semantic call about the nature of the field, not its markup.
aspects.scLimb: Precondition / knowability gate: 'and suggestions for correction are known' (TT DNA: 'suggestions for correction cannot be provided because they are not knowable').
aspects.whyUncovered: Per the survey the knowability gate is uncovered: no ACT rule/test distinguishes a field whose correction is inferable from one where it is not. Automated tools have no concept of whether a correction is computable for a given field; they cannot tell an enumerable 'month' field (suggestion knowable, absence is a fail) from a free-text 'feedback' field (suggestion not knowable, absence is fine). The distinction is entirely about meaning and field semantics.

references.quote: Based on the type of input required, suggestions for correction **cannot be provided** because they are not knowable.
If an input error is automatically detected and suggestions for correction are known, then the suggestions are provided to the user
the intent of this success criterion is to ensure that users receive appropriate suggestions for correction of an input error if it is possible.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build PASS pages where a genuinely free-form / un-inferable field rejects only emptiness and shows a generic message (no specific suggestion is possible, so this is conformant). To force the gate judgment, contrast on one page an enumerable field (suggestion knowable -> absence is a FAIL) with a free-form field (suggestion not knowable -> generic message PASSES), each showing only 'Required'.
suggestedScenarios: Required free-text 'Reason for return' textarea whose only error is 'This field is required' — correction not knowable, PASS.
Open 'Display name' field that rejects only emptiness; generic 'Please enter a display name' is sufficient because no specific value is inferable — PASS.
Contrast page: a 'Month' text field (enumerable, must suggest) next to a 'Comments' field (free-form, need not), both showing only 'Required' — judge must FAIL only the Month field.
A 'verification code we emailed you' field where the system cannot know the code to suggest — generic error is conformant, PASS.
A hand-typed full-legal-name field where the only knowable rule is non-empty; generic message PASSES.
A 'choose a unique URL slug' field where the system DOES know availability and could suggest alternatives — here absence of a suggestion IS a FAIL, contrasted with the genuinely-unknowable cases.

aspects.title: Suggestion technically present but too vague/generic to actually let the user fix the error
aspects.description: The error message contains language that gestures at a fix but is so generic it does not give the user enough to actually correct the input: 'Please check your entry and try again', 'That doesn't look right — please fix it', 'Enter a valid value', 'Improve your input.' A presence-of-text check passes and even a 'does it mention fixing?' heuristic may pass, yet the user still cannot determine WHAT to change. Trusted Tester requires the description to contain ADEQUATE information for the user to know what is required to fix the error; vague filler fails that bar. The judgment is whether the words, in this field's context, are actionable — distinct from the 'wrong/misleading' aspect (which is confidently specific but false) and from the 'no suggestion' aspect (which has no fix language at all).
aspects.scLimb: Adequacy threshold of the suggestion: 'The description contains adequate information for the user to know what is required to fix the error' / 'sufficient details for how to correct the error.'
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT case exists. Even a presence heuristic that scans for fix-oriented phrasing ('please correct', 'try again') is satisfied by vague filler. Judging whether the suggestion actually conveys what to change — given the specific field's constraints — is a semantic adequacy call no automated tool can make; 'Enter a valid value' is a syntactically valid suggestion but conveys nothing.

references.quote: The description contains adequate information for the user to know what is required to fix the error.
Determine whether guidance provides **sufficient details** for how to correct the error and/or offers suggestions of corrected input.
Where errors are detected, suggest known ways to correct them.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Render error messages that USE fix-oriented language but carry no field-specific content, on fields whose correct constraint is clearly knowable (so adequacy, not knowability, is the failing axis). Pair each with a PASS twin that replaces the filler with concrete guidance (the format, the range, an example), so the judge separates 'mentions fixing' from 'tells you how.'
suggestedScenarios: Date field error 'Please check your entry and try again.' with no format hint — vague, FAIL; PASS twin says 'Use MM/DD/YYYY, e.g. 03/14/2026.'
Email field error 'That doesn't look right — please fix it.' — gestures at a fix but conveys nothing actionable, FAIL.
Password field error 'Improve your password.' on a field with a concrete (knowable) rule set never surfaced — FAIL.
Numeric field 'Enter a valid value.' where the field accepts only 1-10 — generic filler instead of the range, FAIL.
Phone field 'Invalid — please correct and resubmit.' where a 10-digit format is required but never stated — FAIL.
Postal-code field 'Something's wrong with this field.' versus a PASS twin 'Enter a 5-digit ZIP, e.g. 90210.'

aspects.title: Suggestion present but stranded far from its field with no proximity, association, or jump mechanism (locatability of the fix)
aspects.description: The page contains a correct, adequate suggestion for the erroring field, but it is placed where the user cannot reasonably connect it to or reach the field: a correct 'Use MM/DD/YYYY' tip buried in a footer while the date field is at the top; a top-of-page error summary that names the fix but offers no working link to jump to the field and no near-field repetition; or a suggestion placed inside the wrong section so it reads as belonging to a different field. G177 and G139 make proximity/locatability part of HOW the suggestion must be provided. Whether the suggestion is close enough, associated with the right field, or reachable is a visual/spatial and contextual judgment about the rendered page, not a property of any single element.
aspects.scLimb: Provision/locatability limb: the suggestion must be 'provided to the user' in a way they can find and connect to the right field (G177 proximity, G139 jump mechanism, G84 'ways to locate the field(s) with a problem easily').
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT case exists, and the survey notes proximity/locatability is covered only as authoring techniques with manual procedures. Automated tools can confirm the suggestion string exists somewhere in the DOM but cannot judge whether it is positioned close enough, visually/semantically associated with the right field, or reachable via a working jump link — these are layout/relevance judgments. A scanner sees the text and passes; a human sees a suggestion stranded far from its field or pointing at the wrong one.

references.quote: Suggestions or links to the suggestions should be placed close to the form fields they are associated with, such as at the top of the form, preceding the form fields, or next to the form fields requiring correction.
a link to that error is provided so that the user does not have to search for it.
describes the nature of the problem, and provides ways to locate the field(s) with a problem easily.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Each FAIL renders a correct, adequate suggestion that is mis-located: physically distant, mis-associated (printed under the wrong field/section), hidden in a collapsed region, or reachable only via a broken anchor. Keep the suggestion TEXT correct so the failing axis is locatability/association alone. Include a PASS twin per family where the same suggestion sits immediately next to the field or has a working jump link.
suggestedScenarios: Long signup form: the date field is at the top, but its correct 'Use MM/DD/YYYY' suggestion is rendered in a footer block after the submit button.
Top-of-page error summary listing 'Email format is wrong — use name@example.com' with no anchor link to the email field and no message near the field itself.
Multi-section form where the suggestion for a section-1 field is printed inside section-3's panel, reading as if it belongs to a different field.
Error summary whose 'jump to field' links all point to a wrong/nonexistent fragment id, so the suggestion is named but unreachable.
A correct did-you-mean suggestion displayed only inside a collapsed accordion the user is never told to open.
PASS twin: an otherwise identical page where the same suggestion is placed immediately next to the field, to verify proximity (not mere presence) is being judged.

aspects.title: Color/asterisk/icon-only error indication with no text suggestion — the 'in text' limb
aspects.description: The page communicates that a field is in error and what to do purely through non-text means: turning the label red, adding a red asterisk, swapping in a warning icon, or showing a red border — with NO text description of the problem or the correction. G84 explicitly states this is insufficient: an asterisk or red label does not satisfy the SC; a text description is required. The judgment is visual and semantic: confirm that the red/icon is the ONLY carrier of the error+fix information and that no equivalent text suggestion accompanies it. The 3.3.3-specific limb is the missing CORRECTION TEXT, distinct from the 1.4.1 'use of color' / 3.3.1 'error identification' framings.
aspects.scLimb: The 'in text' provision: a text description/suggestion is required; non-text indicators (asterisk, red label, icon, border) do not satisfy the SC (G84).
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT case exists for 3.3.3, and while a generic 1.4.1 'use of color' scanner might flag the red, it cannot determine that the missing element is specifically a TEXT SUGGESTION for correction (the 3.3.3 obligation) rather than just identification. Confirming there is no accompanying correction text anywhere, and that the visual carries the whole job, requires reading the rendered page and judging meaning.

references.quote: it is not sufficient simply to indicate that a field has an error by putting an asterisk on its label or turning the label red. A text description of the problem should be provided.
Users who are blind or have impaired vision understand more easily the nature of the input error and how to correct it.
information about the nature and location of the input error is provided in text to enable the users to identify the problem.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Pre-render the post-submit state where invalid fields are signaled ONLY by color/asterisk/icon/border and no correction text exists anywhere in the DOM (verify there is no off-screen or visually-hidden text suggestion). Provide a PASS twin that keeps the same visual but adds the required correction text alongside, so the judge fails only the text-absent version. Keep icon alt/aria empty so the visual is genuinely the sole carrier.
suggestedScenarios: Post-submit form where invalid fields get only a red border and a red label, with zero text anywhere describing the problem or fix.
Fields whose error is shown solely by swapping the label to a red warning-triangle icon with empty alt/aria and no text.
A form that turns the field background pink on error and relies on that alone; the only 'guidance' is an unrelated icon legend elsewhere.
A required field marked with a red asterisk only; on submit the asterisk just intensifies in red — no correction text appears.
A password 'strength meter' that goes red on a weak password with no text rules — color-only correction guidance.
PASS twin: identical page that adds 'Date must be MM/DD/YYYY' text alongside the red border, to verify the judge fails only the text-absent version.

pages.scenario: Travis County homestead-exemption form, post-submit error state. Date-of-birth field holds a real but misshapen value (3-7-1965); server accepts only MM/DD/YYYY. The associated error reads only 'Invalid date.' with no format, example, or hint anywhere on the page, though the correction is trivially knowable.
pages.mechanism: Bare restatement of a format error: the message names the error in text (3.3.1 passes) but omits the knowable fixed accepted format (MM/DD/YYYY), so a screen-reader/cognitive user is told THAT it is wrong but never HOW to fix it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every structural facet passes (label resolves, aria-describedby resolves to a non-empty string, aria-invalid=true, role=alert summary, ~7:1 contrast). 'Invalid date.' and 'Invalid date — use MM/DD/YYYY' are both valid non-empty strings correctly wired to the field; no checker reads the value + the field's fixed accepted format + the message together to judge that a correction is knowable yet absent. That is semantic judgment, not a linter rule.

citation.quote: Provide examples of the correct data entry for the field, Describe the correct data entry for the field, Show values of the correct data entry that are similar to the user's data entry

pages.scenario: Lumen Hall box-office reservation card (the deliberate PASS twin of case-01), post-submit error state. The performance-date field (value 7/4/2025, missing leading zero) accepts only MM/DD/YYYY, but the error SUPPLIES the knowable correction in text: 'Use a two-digit month and day with a four-digit year — MM/DD/YYYY (for example, 07/04/2025).'
pages.mechanism: The error message both describes the required format AND gives a worked example matching the user's intent, so the suggestion of corrected input is provided to the user — satisfying the 3.3.3 obligation that case-01 violates.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the crux of the aspect: an automated checker scores case-01 (fail) and case-02 (pass) IDENTICALLY because every structural facet is the same (label, resolved aria-describedby, aria-invalid, contrast). The only thing separating pass from fail is whether the non-empty string contains an actionable correction versus a restatement — meaning no axe/WAVE/Lighthouse rule reads.

citation.quote: Where errors are detected, suggest known ways to correct them.

pages.scenario: Cadence HR workspace-creation form, post-submit error state. verdicts.cdpEvidence:
CITATION VERIFIED VERBATIM against wcag-techniques/general/G177.html: part 1 ("The objective of this technique is to suggest correct text where the information supplied by the user is not accepted and possible correct text is known.") = line 4 exactly; part 2 ("Suggestions or links to the suggestions should be placed close to the form fields they are associated with, such as at the top of the form, preceding the form fields, or next to the form fields requiring correction.") = line 5 exactly. Both in the Description section; the '...' correctly bridges two non-adjacent sentences of the same technique; supports the claimed mechanism.

CODE (HTML lines 61-75): input#start has aria-invalid="true" aria-describedby="start-err", value="Aug 25 2026" (rejected MM/DD/YYYY input); p.errmsg#start-err (lines 72-74) = "Enter the term start date as MM/DD/YYYY — for example, 08/25/2026." States the required format AND a concrete worked example, placed immediately adjacent to the field. The red triangle SVG (lines 64-68) is aria-hidden="true" focusable="false" — redundant visual only.

RAW AX TREE (inspect.js, backendNodeId 30) confirms the mechanism: role=textbox, name="Term start date", value="Aug 25 2026", description="Enter the term start date as MM/DD/YYYY — for example, 08/25/2026.", invalid="true". So AT receives invalid-state + the resolved suggestion text independent of colour — exactly the documented outcome. SELECTOR ax block: role=textbox, name="Term start date". jsErrors:[], ok:true, lang=en, title present, no external resources (SVG inline). Tab order: course->start->advisor->button, all with visible focus outline rgb(0,95,204); start border 2px solid rgb(178,43,57) = redundant red. Outcome 'passed' is correct under SC 3.3.3 (G84/G85/G177). requiresHumanJudgment=true: a scanner can see aria-describedby resolves to non-empty text but cannot verify the text is a CORRECT, useful correction vs. e.g. 'Invalid date' — the semantic content is the pass/fail discriminator, which is why the icon/colour-only twins evade axe/WAVE/Lighthouse.

problems: MINOR citation defect in case-01.md (not in the prompt's named citation): the .md presents 'the user enters a date in the wrong format;' inside quotation marks attributed to wcag-understanding/error-suggestion.html (Intent), but that exact string does NOT appear in the file. The actual Intent text (line 28-30) reads 'information that is provided by the user but that falls outside the required data format or allowed values.' This is a fabricated/paraphrased verbatim-quote and should be corrected or marked as paraphrase.

MINOR: the .md's second understanding.html quote ('If the user enters 12, ...') uses straight quotes and an ellipsis to stitch the 'Suggestions from a Limited Set of Values' example; the source uses curly quotes ('12,' and 'Do you mean December?'). Faithful elision, acceptable, but not character-for-character verbatim.

G85 citation (the one NAMED in the prompt) verifies VERBATIM at G85.html lines 7-9; the trusted-tester citation verifies VERBATIM at sc-3.3.3-error-suggestion.md lines 24-25. The core citations are sound.

None that affect validity. This is a deliberate PASS twin (no accessibility defect by design); 'errorIsReal=true' is read as 'the claimed PASS mechanism genuinely holds', and 'severity=none' reflects that there is no real issue (as intended).

Minor (non-defect): the primary Understanding citation 'Where errors are detected, suggest known ways to correct them.' is from the 'In brief / What to do' summary box, which is guidance-intent rather than normative SC text; however it is verbatim, correctly attributed, and supports the mechanism. The G85 and Trusted-Tester citations carry the normative weight and both verify verbatim.

MD-DOC CITATION DEFECT (does not affect the prompt's authoritative citation): the .md doc (lines 30-35) cites 'wcag-understanding/error-suggestion.html' with two quotes, but that file does NOT exist anywhere in refs/ (only refs/trusted-tester/sc-3.3.3-error-suggestion.md is present) and neither quoted sentence appears anywhere in refs/. The path is broken/unverifiable.

The md doc's second quote 'Where errors are detected, suggest known ways to correct them.' is a paraphrase, not the verbatim WCAG Understanding 'In brief' wording. Quote #1 ('...may find it difficult to understand how to correct the errors.') is genuine WCAG Intent text but still cites a non-existent local file.

Minor doc imprecision: docs say 'summertime' violates three of four rules; it actually violates all four (length 10 < 12 fails minLength too, plus no uppercase/digit/symbol). Does not change the verdict (>=1 detected error with knowable, withheld suggestion).

Minor (non-defect) AT-value quirk: the spinbutton's aria-valuenow=24 (line 96) is out of the declared 1..10 bounds, so Chromium clamps the AX-exposed numeric value to 10 ('value': 10 in the AX tree) while the visible static text child reads '24'. This sighted-vs-AT value mismatch is a real curiosity but is orthogonal to the 3.3.3 mechanism and does not weaken the verdict.

The +/- spinbutton buttons (lines 91, 99) are aria-hidden + tabindex=-1 and there is no JS, so the control cannot actually be incremented/decremented. This is acceptable for a hand-authored static post-submit error snapshot but means the widget is non-functional as a real spinbutton; reviewers should know the page is a frozen error state, not an interactive control.

Borderline-by-design (not a defect): under the bare letter of SC 3.3.3 a suggestion IS provided, so a literalist reading could argue 'passed'; the 'failed' verdict correctly rests on SC intent + G177 'correct text' + TT 'suggestions for CORRECTED input' — a suggestion the same field deterministically rejects is not a valid correction. Sound intent-based judgment, appropriate for a human-judgment corpus.

Minor cosmetic: the scenario narration/HTML comment use entered code 'SAVE20'; no functional impact since SPRING20 (the expired suggested value) carries the failure and is consistent throughout the code and table.

MINOR / SC-fit nuance (not a fabrication): SC 3.3.3 is conditional on an input error being DETECTED, where 'input error' = information NOT accepted by the system (Understanding intent, line 25-30). Here '07' IS accepted (probe confirms aria-invalid stays null; the form submits it as July). With no detected input error, a purist ACT reviewer could argue 3.3.3 is INAPPLICABLE and the defect is closer to a false-error (3.3.1) or general-usability/4.1.3 problem. The corpus's own bucket framing ('suggestion present but wrong or misleading') makes 'failed' defensible, so I keep the label, but the doc should acknowledge the SC-precondition tension rather than present it as a clean textbook 3.3.3 failure.

The doc/comment overstates the automated-tool baseline slightly ('axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a present, associated suggestion' and pass it) — true, but worth noting the live region only ever contains text, never sets aria-invalid, so there is genuinely nothing for a checker to flag. This strengthens (not weakens) requiresHumanJudgment.
None. This is a correctly-constructed PASS twin. errorIsReal=false is the intended state: there is no accessibility defect to detect. The documented outcome (passed) is correct.

None material. This is a PASS case (documented expected outcome 'passed', failure-mechanism explicitly NONE). 'errorIsReal=true' is reported in the sense that the page genuinely realizes its documented conformant state, not that a defect exists — there is no defect, which is exactly the claim. If the harness interprets errorIsReal strictly as 'a defect exists', this should be read as false; the substantive judgment is that the page correctly PASSES.

Minor: the .md offers TWO citation blocks; the normative-text quote (lines 4-5 of ref) and the DNA-exception quote (lines 15-16). Both are verbatim-accurate, so no problem — noted only for completeness.

Minor (non-defect) nuance, not affecting the verdict: #confirm-error uses role="alert" but the page is a STATIC post-submit snapshot, so the alert is never dynamically inserted and would not actually fire a live-region announcement in a real session. The verdict survives because the same error text is also wired to the role=group via aria-describedby (CDP DESC confirms it is in the group's accessible description), so the correction is perceivable on field navigation regardless of live-region timing.

Terminology note: this is a PASS limb ('error is real' in the sense that the documented conformant behavior genuinely holds; there is NO accessibility defect on the page). The page correctly tests that withholding a secret-revealing suggestion is conformant under the 3.3.3 security/purpose exception.
See above

Citation path-prefix defect (minor): the .md doc cites the G85 quote as 'refs/wcag-techniques/general/G85.html', but the file actually lives at 'wcag-techniques/general/G85.html' (no refs/ prefix). The quoted sentence ('Check that other data previously entered by the user is re-displayed, unless the data is in a security related field...') IS verbatim at line 22 of the real file, and the trusted-tester citations are both verbatim and correctly pathed, so this is cosmetic, not a hallucination.

Note (not a defect): the role=alert exists in the initial static DOM rather than being dynamically inserted, so a screen reader would NOT auto-announce it as a live region. However the message still reaches AT because BOTH inputs are aria-describedby the alert (CDP AX tree shows the full text in each textbox's 'description'), so the conformant outcome holds. This is acceptable for a static post-submit 'saved state' fixture.

Outcome label rests on the spirit/security-clause of SC 3.3.3, not its literal Trusted-Tester 'Evaluate Results' (TT 5.G PASSES if a suggestion is provided OR the description is adequate — and a fluent suggestion IS provided here). A strict TT 5.G run would arguably mark this PASS. The 'failed' verdict is defensible only via the 'jeopardize security' exception + G85's password-redisplay warning, which the .md is candid about. This is acceptable for an adversarial human-judgment corpus but the SC boundary is interpretive, not mechanical.

Secondary (non-blocking) leak adjacent to the claim: the password input carries value="Hawthorne1!" so the tab-order signal exposes the live new-password attempt as the field's accessible name — another over-disclosure vector beyond the #newpw-error element under test (reinforces, does not contradict, the claim).

Minor (not the issue under test): #o6 (HTML line 75) is an empty input with aria-invalid="true" and no accessible name — AX tree shows it as an unlabeled textbox in the group. Peripheral nit; does not affect the 3.3.3 verdict.

None material. This is a deliberate DNA/knowability-gate PASS fixture, so there is intentionally NO accessibility violation present (errorIsReal=false reflects 'no defect', which is the intended state). The documented outcome 'passed' is correct.
Minor: the primary WCAG intent quote is rendered across two wrapped lines (error-suggestion.html lines 25-26) but matches verbatim apart from whitespace — not a defect.

Minor wording slack only (not a defect): the .md (line 5) calls Purchase month 'a free-text input' while the title/HTML/attribute-tuple correctly frame it as a plain TEXT input whose MEANING is enumerable (twelve month names). The intent is unambiguous and consistent — month is markup-free-text but semantically enumerable — so the FAIL gate is sound; the phrasing is just slightly loose.

Primary citation is a faithful stitch of the

lead-in (line 74) and the first

PROMPT/FILE METADATA MISMATCH (review-harness defect): the prompt describes a creator-platform unique-handle scenario (claim 'plinth.co/studio' rejected), selector '#slug', citation G177.html, and claimed expected outcome 'failed'. The claimed 3.3.3 FAIL mechanism (system withholds a KNOWN suggestion from an enumerable pool, as in G177) does not apply to this file: a corrupted-file rejection has no system-knowable correct replacement value, so absence of a suggested value is conformant. The claimed issue is therefore not real for this page.

Minor: the file input '#doc' carries aria-invalid='true' in source (line 102); Chromium serializes the file input as role=button and did not surface the invalid property in the AX dump, but invalid state is present in markup and the error text is exposed via the accessible description, so AT users are informed.

No genuine defect — and that is intended: this is a DNA/knowability-gate PASS case, not a failure case. errorIsReal=false here means 'no accessibility error exists', which is the correct state for the documented 'passed' outcome.

Minor: the .md doc lists two citations; both verify verbatim, but my initial keyword grep for the wcag-understanding intent quote failed because the sentence wraps across lines 25-26 of error-suggestion.html. On reading the file the quote is an exact match — not a defect, noted only for transparency.

Minor framing nuance (not a defect): in strict TT/ACT terms, an error where no suggestion is knowable is formally a DNA / inapplicable for the suggestion obligation. The doc labels it 'passed' and grounds that on TT PASS condition 2 ('description contains adequate information to fix the error'), which IS independently satisfied here, so the 'passed' label is defensible. Reviewers should understand the page passes via the adequate-info path, not because a suggestion was provided.

All three citations verified VERBATIM and on the correct files: TT 5.G DNA quote (refs/trusted-tester/sc-3.3.3-error-suggestion.md L13-14, only a line-wrap whitespace difference), TT PASS condition 2 (same file L25), WCAG Intent quote (wcag-understanding/error-suggestion.html L25). No hallucinated or stitched quotes.

Secondary citations in the .md doc (wcag-understanding/error-suggestion.html and wcag-techniques/general/G85.html) reference files that do NOT exist in the refs tree (only PDFs are present under refs/wcag-understanding/); they cannot be verified verbatim. This is a minor sourcing gap, not a defect in the page, and the prompt's authoritative citation (trusted-tester) is verified.

Minor (non-blocking): aria-describedby="iban-toast" points at the toast container, which is EMPTY at page load and only populated after blur. Pointing describedby at a transient empty live region is unconventional (stable hint text is the usual target). It does not weaken the 3.3.3 verdict — and arguably reinforces the 'announcement is correct, content is inadequate' framing — but it is an authoring oddity worth noting.

Minor (citation hygiene, not a defect): the third quote (trusted-tester DNA 'cannot be provided because they are not knowable') spans a line break in the source (lines 13-14, 'not\n  knowable'); it is verbatim once line-wrap whitespace is normalized, but a naive single-line grep misses it.

No defects found in the citation, outcome label, or self-containment. Minor (non-blocking) note: the page renders a STATIC post-submit error state with no JS validation — intentional and appropriate for the corpus, but the 'on submit it is rendered' framing describes an implied server round-trip rather than runtime behavior; does not affect the verdict.

TASK-PROMPT METADATA MISMATCH (packaging, not file defect): the prompt describes a different page — a 'nonprofit donation form' with a top-of-page email error summary, element under test input#email, citation G139.html. The ACTUAL file on disk is a Cedar County Public Library card-renewal form whose mechanism is an aria-hidden correction box (element div#barcode-fix / input#barcode), cited to error-suggestion.html + G177.html. I reviewed the real file. The desync between the orchestrator's case metadata and the actual file should be reconciled.

Minor robustness nit (does NOT change the verdict): the footer 'Cedar County Public Library · 14-digit card numbers are printed on the back of every card.' IS present in the AX tree, so the literal '14-digit' fact is technically reachable somewhere on the page. It is generic site chrome, not associated with the input error and not presented as the correction, so the suggestion is still not 'provided to the user' for the error; but the MD's stronger framing ('the example 21345000123456 does not appear anywhere in the AX tree' — true; but the 14-digit fact does leak via the footer) is slightly overstated.

Minor cite-targeting nuance (not a defect): the prompt's headline 'Claimed citation' is G84, but G84's verbatim example is about a text description at the TOP of the page that indicates which field erred — it best supports the top-of-page alert situation, not the misplacement mechanism. The mechanism (suggestion placed under the wrong field two sections away) is most precisely covered by G177, which the .md also cites. Both G84 and G177 quotes verify character-for-character, so all citations are sound; G177 is simply the more on-point primary cite.

METADATA MISMATCH (primary defect): The task prompt under review describes a DIFFERENT page than the file. Task claims a 'state tax e-filing form' with a top error summary and broken 'Jump to field' links (summary -> #ein-field/#routing, real ids ein/bank-routing-input), selector a[href="#ein-field"], mechanism G139 broken-jump-link, citation wcag-techniques/general/G139.html. NONE of this exists in case-04.html.

The claimed element under test a[href="#ein-field"] does not exist: grep for 'ein-field|routing|Jump to field|href="#' returns exit 1 (no match); the page contains NO anchor elements at all (only interactive element is the submit button, tabOrder confirms payee->iban->amount->button).

The claimed citation wcag-techniques/general/G139.html and its quote ('a text description at the top of the page... provides a link the field(s) with a problem') are NOT what this page's actual .md doc cites; the doc cites G84.html + error-suggestion.html. The task-supplied citation is therefore mis-attributed to this file.
Consequently the task's claimed mechanism (G139 jump mechanism defeated) is unsound FOR THIS FILE — there is no jump mechanism on the page to defeat.

Note (not a defect): The ACTUAL on-file case-04 is a valid, sound 3.3.3 'failed' case (correct IBAN-fix suggestion locked in a mouse-hover-only title='' on a non-focusable span.info; AX shows role=generic name='' so AT gets nothing; aria-describedby points only at the bare 'This entry can't be processed.'; suggestion appears nowhere else in the DOM). Its three citations (G84 'in text' portion, error-suggestion Intent, error-suggestion 'suggest known ways to correct them') all verify VERBATIM. The file itself is keep-worthy; only the task metadata is wrong.

This is a PASS twin, so by design there is no accessibility defect on the page. errorIsReal=false correctly reflects 'no genuine accessibility error present' — the documented intent is that the page PASSES (proving proximity/locatability). The page genuinely yields the documented 'passed' outcome.

Secondary citation G139 is a STITCHED quote, not verbatim: the doc presents 'provides a link the field(s) with a problem so the user can easily navigate to it to fix the problem' as one sentence, but it fuses G139.html line 4 ('...provides a link the field(s) with a problem') with line 9 ('...so the user can easily navigate to it to fix the problem') — two non-adjacent fragments. Minor: it is a SECONDARY citation (not the task's named primary G177), the underlying jump-mechanism claim is genuinely supported by G139, and the page implements a real working jump link (href=#arrival -> id=arrival).

Nuance on SC scope: the bare normative SC 3.3.3 text ('Where errors are detected, suggest known ways to correct them') does NOT itself mandate proximity/locatability — that is advisory technique G177 ('should be placed close to the form fields'). The PASS verdict is nonetheless correct under BOTH readings (suggestion exists AND is locatable), so the boundary the aspect probes is sound, but the framing slightly overstates locatability as a normative SC limb rather than an advisory technique.

Minor framing overclaim (not disqualifying): the page comment and the .md assert the field is announced 'byte-identical to a valid field' implying only the suggestion limb is at issue, but since there is also NO programmatic error identification at all for AT (no aria-invalid, no message), 3.3.1 is arguably also implicated for screen-reader users. This strengthens rather than weakens the 3.3.3 finding, but the 'distinct from 3.3.1' claim is only partly accurate — the colour-only indication identifies the error to SIGHTED users while leaving AT users with neither identification nor suggestion.

Minor (not a defect): input has min=1 but NO max, so AX tree reports valuemax:0 - the allowed ceiling (5) is not programmatically constrained either; this strengthens the 3.3.3 failure rather than weakening it, no change needed.
Minor: the .md SR-announcement claims (spinbutton, invalid entry) are confirmed accurate by the AX tree; no problem.

Minor SC-overlap nuance (not disqualifying): the page also implicates 3.3.1 Error Identification because the error itself is never programmatically or textually identified (no aria-invalid, no live region, no text). 3.3.3 remains the correct primary SC since the case is specifically about the absent suggestion/correction text, but a reviewer should be aware the same page would also fail 3.3.1.

Cosmetic: a naive substring scan can yield a false 'error text present' positive (the word 'required' appears in marketing copy 'No card required.' and 'password' in the label). Whole-word verification confirms there is genuinely no error/rules/suggestion text — no defect to the case, just a caution against substring-based automated checks.

Minor naming/scenario mismatch: the folder name and md prose say 'asterisk' / 'color-asterisk', but the actual error cue is a warning-triangle SVG icon, not an asterisk. Outcome is unaffected because G84 treats icon-only and colour-only error indication identically, but the label is imprecise.

Belt-and-suspenders attribute combo on the SVG (role='img' + aria-label='' + aria-hidden='true' + focusable='false'). aria-hidden='true' alone already removes it from the AX tree (inspect confirms selector ax:null); the empty aria-label on role='img' is redundant. Does not affect the verdict.

MINOR (does not affect verdict): The .md/.html claim 'the required asterisk is injected via CSS ::after content, which most screen readers do not announce' overstates Chromium's behavior. The raw AX tree folds the ::after ' *' INTO the accessible name (nid textbox name = 'رقم الهوية الوطنية *'). So in Chromium the asterisk IS exposed. The mechanism still holds because (a) the asterisk carries no correction-suggestion text, and (b) the errored field announces identically to the two valid fields (all three names carry the same ' *'), so the AX tree distinguishes the bad field in no way at all.

OBSERVATION (not a defect): AX 'required:false' on #nid is correct — there is no required/aria-required attribute, so the visual asterisk is the only required signal, which actually strengthens the symbol-only critique.

None material. This is a PASS twin and is correctly constructed/labeled. Minor (non-defect) note: #start-err renders as a plain `paragraph` in the AX tree, not a live region / role=alert; irrelevant for the documented post-submit static-render scenario since the text reaches AT via the resolved aria-describedby `description`, which is all SC 3.3.3 requires.
